{"id": "44:56/q02", "question": "How is the clause ‘they do not taste’ attached grammatically?", "turns_on": "Which earlier pronoun or clause supplies the circumstance, or whether this sentence stands independently.", "positions": [{"id": "44:56/q02/p1", "position": "It is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in ‘secure’ (āminīn).", "reasons": "Al-Samīn gives this antecedent for the circumstantial clause."}, {"id": "44:56/q02/p2", "position": "It is a second or third circumstantial clause from the object of ‘We paired them’ (zawwajnāhum).", "reasons": "Al-Samīn gives this alternative and also records ways of attaching the preceding āminīn to yadʿūn, an earlier circumstantial clause, or an independent clause."}, {"id": "44:56/q02/p3", "position": "The clause may be independent.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī leaves both independence and circumstantial attachment open."}, {"id": "44:56/q02/p4", "position": "The clause may be circumstantial, with its precise attachment left open.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī mentions the circumstantial possibility without choosing an antecedent; Ibn ʿĀshūr calls it an added circumstantial clause promising lasting bliss."}]}

{"id": "44:56/q04", "question": "What does tasting death mean here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "44:56/q04/p1", "position": "It figuratively describes undergoing death and its painful causes, as though tasting unpleasant food.", "reasons": "Scholars cited by al-Wāḥidī and al-Qurṭubī say death is an accident and cannot literally be tasted; al-Ṭabrisī compares it to disliked food. {"id": "44:56/q05", "question": "What life does the denial of death promise the people of Paradise?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "44:56/q05/p1", "position": "They live in Paradise permanently and never die there.", "reasons": "Muqātil, al-Ṭabarī, al-Zajjāj, al-Wāḥidī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Nasafī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Biqāʿī, Bursevî, al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī, Asad and the Study Quran state the assurance. Al-Rāzī says it follows the enumeration of pleasures; al-Wāḥidī, al-Ṭabrisī and Ibn ʿĀshūr say it secures enjoyment from death's interruption, though people in Hell also do not simply die. Bursevî lists no aging, sleep, fear, day or night, darkness, heat, cold or exit; Iṣlāḥī adds unwithheld fruit and safety from fear. Al-Biqāʿī says even death's onset is absent and complete bliss follows resurrection. Al-Samīn's Ibn ʿAṭiyya explains that only worldly death occurred; Ibn Kathīr calls the exception a reinforcement of this negation."}]}
{"id": "44:56/q06", "question": "How does the exception of the first death work?", "turns_on": "Whether an exception from a future denial can name a past worldly death; the attested sense of illā; whether the exception must be connected; and whether the dying are already in Paradise by anticipation.", "positions": [{"id": "44:56/q06/p1", "position": "It is disconnected or means ‘but’: they already tasted worldly death, with none in Paradise.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās says the accusative exception is outside the preceding category. Al-Qurṭubī cites Sībawayh's poetry for disconnected exception; al-Samīn, Ibn Kathīr, al-Zarkashī, Bursevî and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī give this analysis. Al-Wāḥidī, al-Rāzī and al-Nasafī phrase it as ‘but they already tasted it.’ Al-Dāmghānī calls it a resumptive exception and cites 92:19, 88:23, 95:6, 72:28 and 34:23. The objectors cited by Ibn Qutayba compare excluding yesterday's gift from today's giving; al-Ālūsī says the first death happened before Paradise, and prefers connection unless evidence requires disconnection. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī objects that this does not explain the word ‘first.’"}, {"id": "44:56/q06/p2", "position": "Illā means ‘other than’ or ‘apart from’: no death beyond the one already undergone.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba, al-Zajjāj, al-Wāḥidī, al-Baghawī, al-Ṭabrisī, Ibn al-Jawzī, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Samīn's Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Ālūsī and Asad invoke the exception at 4:22; Ibn al-Jawzī also mentions 11:107, and Asad compares 37:58–59. Al-Wāḥidī transmits al-Farrāʾ's account of an exception adding rather than subtracting. Al-Ṭabrisī prefers an adjectival or substitute construction meaning ghayr, since ghayr is an adverb but illā a particle and the first death has passed. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī prefers apposition for the past death and denial of barzakh or Garden death, but says this analysis alone does not explain ‘first.’ Al-Ṭabarī objects that ‘other than’ would imply a further death; Abū Ḥayyān and Ibn ʿAṭiyya reject his objection as the meaning is coherent. Al-Ālūsī says excluding the past first death from future deaths removes the paradox."}, {"id": "44:56/q06/p3", "position": "Illā has the sense ‘after’: they taste no death after the first.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī prefers this from a closeness of meanings and says Arabic may substitute illā for baʿda; he uses 4:22 and analogies of rajāʾ meaning fear in Abū Dhuʾayb and zannū meaning knowledge in another poet. Al-Thaʿlabī compares ‘no food today except what I ate yesterday’; al-Baghawī allows ‘after’ as well as ‘apart from.’ Al-Samīn reports the majority reject this because the proposed sense of illā is unattested; al-Ālūsī says most commentators do not recognize it."}, {"id": "44:56/q06/p4", "position": "The exception is attached to an impossible future repetition of a past death, emphatically denying any death.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī's explanation is quoted by al-Rāzī, al-Samīn and al-Zarkashī; al-Bayḍāwī, al-Biqāʿī, Bursevî, al-Ālūsī and Ibn ʿĀshūr also use the impossible condition. Al-Samīn calls it negation by an impossible proof and cites al-Nābigha's sword-notches as an impossible flaw. Al-Zarkashī compares the camel passing through a needle's eye, which has no actual endpoint; he notes a poet's still stronger emaciation hyperbole but says that gives no license to match the Qurʾān. Al-Ālūsī compares the offer of water ‘only embers’ and 4:22; Ibn ʿĀshūr recalls 44:35. Al-Ālūsī prefers the interpretation; al-Biqāʿī says even death's first onset is denied."}, {"id": "44:56/q06/p5", "position": "The exception is connected because a believer already approaches or sees Paradise at worldly death.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba says the blessed encounter comfort in differing degrees, including spirit and fragrance, an opened gate and martyrs' spirits in green birds; a quoted poet uses taʿallaqa for eating, and Jaʿfar b. Abī Ṭālib is depicted flying with two wings among angels. Al-Wāḥidī, al-Baghawī, Ibn al-Jawzī and al-Qurṭubī likewise say the dying see their dwellings, angels, provision or blessings and so are associated with Paradise. Al-Samīn speaks of vision of its promise or certainty of its bliss; al-Zarkashī treats this as one of three explanations, with ‘tasting’ figurative. Al-Biqāʿī extends its causes into life and posthumous enjoyment. Al-Ālūsī reports it as a connected reading. Ibn Qutayba's Kitāb Gharīb directs the reader to his Mushkil treatment."}, {"id": "44:56/q06/p6", "position": "The exception is connected because death is the first state of the afterlife.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī gives this option. Al-Ālūsī reports it but argues that it fragments the sentence and calls for figurative language. Al-Ālūsī also notes the objection that a past worldly death cannot be tasted later in Paradise unless a negative exception affirms the excluded item there; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī raises both the apparent implication of dying in Paradise and the past-versus-future problem."}]}

{"id": "44:56/q10", "question": "What do reports say about the end of death and the life of Paradise?", "turns_on": "The reports describe different promised features and events; no source presents them as competing accounts.", "positions": [{"id": "44:56/q10/p1", "position": "Death is brought as a speckled ram and slaughtered between Paradise and Hell; both groups are told there is no more death.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr says this report occurs in both Ṣaḥīḥ collections."}, {"id": "44:56/q10/p2", "position": "Paradise's people retain health, life, ease and youth without illness, death, hardship or aging.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr attributes this prophetic report to Abū Saʿīd and Abū Hurayra and says Muslim transmits it."}, {"id": "44:56/q10/p3", "position": "Whoever fears God enters Paradise and lives without death, worn clothing or fading youth.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr reports this from Abū Hurayra from the Prophet."}, {"id": "44:56/q10/p4", "position": "Paradise's people do not sleep, because sleep is death's sibling.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr gives Jābir's prophetic report; for one route al-Bazzār says only al-Thawrī narrated from Ibn al-Munkadir and only al-Firyābī from al-Thawrī, while Ibn Kathīr notes another route. {"id": "44:56/q11", "question": "What does ‘He protected them from the punishment of Hell’ mean?", "turns_on": "Whether the Fire is read as afterlife punishment or as an inward image of deprivation from God.", "positions": [{"id": "44:56/q11/p1", "position": "God guards the blessed from Hell's punishment and harm.", "reasons": "Muqātil, al-Baghawī, al-Ṭabrisī, al-Nasafī, al-Biqāʿī, Bursevî, al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī and Asad state the protection; Bursevî and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī define wiqāya as warding off harm. The Study Quran relates it to mercy preceding wrath, cites 52:18, and quotes the Prophet's comparison: God is more tender to His servants than a mother protecting her child from fire."}, {"id": "44:56/q11/p2", "position": "In an inward reading, the Fire signifies deprivation through distance from God and abandonment.", "reasons": "Bursevî gives this allusion. {"id": "44:56/q14", "question": "Why is protection from Hell mentioned after Paradise's blessings?", "turns_on": "Whether the sequence is understood as reversing the temporal order of salvation or as naming two kinds of hardship.", "positions": [{"id": "44:56/q14/p1", "position": "Though logically prior to attaining Paradise, the wording mentions protection afterward while indicating God protected them from the outset.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī explicitly raises and answers the ordering problem."}, {"id": "44:56/q14/p2", "position": "The clauses complete a twofold removal of hardship: death changes abode or state, while Hell changes joy to misery.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī explains the sequence through the two hardships excluded."}]}

{"id": "44:58/q01", "question": "How does the opening fāʾ connect this verse to what precedes?", "turns_on": "Which part of the clause the fāʾ is taken to introduce.", "positions": [{"id": "44:58/q01/p1", "position": "It draws a conclusion from the preceding argument and returns to the Book announced at the sūra’s opening.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says the fāʾ summarizes the sūra’s aims in their order and recalls the Book of 44:2–3. {"id": "44:58/q03", "question": "What does the object of ‘We made it easy’ refer to?", "turns_on": "Whether the implicit object is identified as the Book itself or, more specifically, its comprehension.", "positions": [{"id": "44:58/q03/p1", "position": "The pronoun denotes the Qur’an or Book, understood though unspoken here.", "reasons": "Thaʿlabī, Baghawī and Ṭabrisī make the unspoken Qur’an explicit. Rāzī calls it the opening’s clear, beneficial Book; Qurṭubī says the close urges adherence to this unnamed Qur’an."}, {"id": "44:58/q03/p2", "position": "What is understood as the omitted object is comprehension of the Qur’an.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says the omitted noun is supplied by context and identifies the ease specifically with comprehension."}]}
{"id": "44:58/q04", "question": "In what sense did God make the Qur’an easy?", "turns_on": "Whether ease names intelligible Arabic, facilitated recitation, or suitability for teaching despite complex content; Iṣlāḥī explicitly disputes a merely bland sense.", "positions": [{"id": "44:58/q04/p1", "position": "He made it accessible for understanding and remembrance through clear Arabic suited to its audience.", "reasons": "Muqātil and Wāḥidī speak of ease through Muḥammad’s tongue. Kashshāf, Rāzī, Bayḍāwī, Nasafī, Bursevī, Ālūsī, Elmalılı, Ṭabāṭabāʾī and Kuran Yolu connect ease with Arabic and intelligibility; the last says it lacks tangled expressions or concepts beyond its audience. Ibn Kathīr calls the language supremely eloquent and lucid. Asad says revelation is understandable in the Prophet’s human tongue. {"id": "44:58/q13", "question": "What recitation merits are reported for Sūrat al-Dukhān?", "turns_on": "The reports differ in the time of recitation and in the promised benefit.", "positions": [{"id": "44:58/q13/p1", "position": "Reciting it at night brings seventy thousand angels seeking forgiveness for the reciter by morning.", "reasons": "Baghawī and Kashshāf both transmit this report from the Prophet; Kashshāf names the sūra Ḥā Mīm al-Dukhān."}, {"id": "44:58/q13/p2", "position": "Reciting the sūra mentioning the Smoke on Friday night brings forgiveness by morning.", "reasons": "Kashshāf reports this as another Prophetic promise."}]}

{"id": "46:4/q03", "question": "How is أَرَءَيْتُم read?", "turns_on": "How the hamza is retained, softened, deleted, or supplemented with kaf.", "positions": [{"id": "46:4/q03/p1", "position": "A reading adds kaf: araʾaytkum or araytkum.", "reasons": "Farra reports Abdullah's practice also at 107:1; Jishumi identifies Ibn Masud's codex; Alusi records the variant."}, {"id": "46:4/q03/p2", "position": "The common reading is araʾaytum.", "reasons": "Jishumi cites regional codices; Nahhas calls araytum a familiar Arabic reduction of original araʾaytum and notes another dialect softens the second hamza."}, {"id": "46:4/q03/p3", "position": "A reading deletes the hamza.", "reasons": "Zajjaj records omitted alif; Qiraat-ER calls deletion a mutawatir Hijazi simplification from raʾa to raytum."}, {"id": "46:4/q03/p4", "position": "A mutawatir reading softens the hamza to an intermediate sound.", "reasons": "Qiraat-ER distinguishes this from deletion."}, {"id": "46:4/q03/p5", "position": "A mutawatir reading lengthens the vowel before the hamza.", "reasons": "Qiraat-ER notes its deliberative prosody."}]}
